name: Pādma mahākalpa (past)
description: Traditional chronology: the great kalpa called Pādma that closed the first half (parārdha) of Brahmā's hundred-year life, according to the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
sources.quote: ekam asya vyatītaṃ tu parārdhaṃ brahmaṇo 'nagha / tasyānte 'bhūn mahākalpaḥ pādma ity abhiviśrutaḥ

note: Brahmā's full life (para) is a hundred of his years (ViP 1.3.5). Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Vārāha kalpa (current day of Brahmā)
description: Traditional chronology: the present day of Brahmā, the first kalpa of the second parārdha, named after the Boar (ViP 1.3.28); a day of Brahmā is a thousand caturyugas (Manu 1.72; ViP 1.3.15; BhP 3.11.22), followed by a night of equal length.

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

note: Human-year figure computed as 1,000 × 4,320,000 using the 360:1 ratio implied by ViP 1.3.19–21; Manu gives only divine yugas. Āryabhaṭa instead makes a day of Brahmā 1,008 yugas (AB 3.8). Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Svāyambhuva manvantara (1st)
description: Traditional chronology: the first of the fourteen manvantaras of the present kalpa, under Svāyambhuva Manu (ViP 3.1.6), in which Dhruva, son of Uttānapāda, lived (ViP 1.11).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
GRETIL e-text (U. Stiehl), vulgate numbering

note: Each manvantara is 'a little over seventy-one' caturyugas (ViP 1.3.18; BhP 3.11.24); ViP 1.3.19–21 gives 852,000 divine and 306,720,000 human years 'without the excess'. Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Cākṣuṣa manvantara (6th)
description: Traditional chronology: the sixth manvantara, at whose end the deluge of the Matsya story occurs according to the Matsya Purāṇa (2.14) and the Bhāgavata (1.3.15); the Bhāgavata also places the churning of the ocean in this period (recall).

Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Vaivasvata manvantara (7th, current)
description: Traditional chronology: the present, seventh manvantara of Vaivasvata (Śrāddhadeva) Manu, son of Vivasvat, with Purandara as Indra and the seven sages Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, Atri, Jamadagni, Gautama, Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja (ViP 3.1.30–32; BhP 8.13.1–5); Vāmana is born in it (BhP 8.13.6).

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

name: Sāvarṇika manvantara (8th, future)
description: Traditional chronology: the coming eighth manvantara, whose Manu Sāvarṇi will be King Suratha by the Goddess's boon; the Devī Māhātmya is framed as 'in the Sāvarṇika manvantara' (MkP colophons) and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa describes the future manvantaras (3.2).

name: Mahāyuga (caturyuga)
description: Traditional chronology: the cycle of Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, totalling 12,000 divine years (Manu 1.71; ViP 1.3.11; BhP 3.11.18); computed as 4,320,000 human years where one divine year = 360 human years.

Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Twenty-eighth mahāyuga of the Vaivasvata manvantara (current)
description: Traditional chronology: the present caturyuga, the twenty-eighth of the seventh manvantara: the Matsya places Vedavyāsa's birth in the twenty-eighth Dvāpara (47.245), and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa lists twenty-eight Vyāsas of successive Dvāparas (3.3, recall).

name: Kṛta (Satya) yuga
description: Traditional chronology: the first and best age, dharma standing on four feet: 4,000 divine years with dawn and dusk of 400 each = 4,800 (Manu 1.69; ViP 1.3.12–13), i.e. 1,728,000 human years at 360:1. The Rāmāyaṇa sets the churning of the ocean 'formerly in the Kṛta age' (VR CE 1.44.14); tradition places Narasiṃha's killing of Hiraṇyakaśipu in this age (the Matsya's '4th yuga' wording at 47.237 is ambiguous).

name: Tretā yuga
description: Traditional chronology: the second age: 3,000 divine years with junctions of 300 each = 3,600 (1,296,000 human years). The Nārāyaṇīya places Rāma Bhārgava in Tretā (MBh CE 12.326.77); the Matsya places Vāmana in the seventh Tretā (47.239) and Dattātreya, Māndhātṛ and Jāmadagnya in particular Tretās (47.241–243).

name: Junction of Tretā and Dvāpara (Rāma)
description: Traditional chronology: the Nārāyaṇīya foretells that 'at the junction of Tretā and Dvāpara' Viṣṇu will be Rāma Dāśarathi and slay Rāvaṇa (MBh CE 12.326.78–81); the Matsya places Rāma in the twenty-fourth yuga (47.244).

name: Dvāpara yuga
description: Traditional chronology: the third age: 2,000 divine years with junctions of 200 each = 2,400 (864,000 human years); in each Dvāpara a Vyāsa divides the Veda (ViP 3.3, recall; MatsP 47.245).

name: Junction of Dvāpara and Kali (Kṛṣṇa and the Kurukṣetra war)
description: Traditional chronology: the Nārāyaṇīya foretells Kṛṣṇa's birth at Mathurā 'at the final junction of Dvāpara and Kali' (MBh CE 12.326.82); the Kurukṣetra war and the Yādava destruction belong to this junction in tradition, and Kali begins on the day Kṛṣṇa leaves the earth (ViP 4.24.27, 4.24.32; 5.38.8).

sources.edition: BORI Critical Edition (GRETIL e-text)
sources.quote: dvāparasya kaleś caiva saṃdhau paryavasānike / prādurbhāvaḥ kaṃsahetor mathurāyāṃ bhaviṣyati

sources.edition: Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner

note: Tradition equates this junction with the Kali epoch of 3102 BCE (see sac:kali-yuga). Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Kali yuga (current)
description: Traditional chronology: the fourth and present age: 1,000 divine years with junctions of 100 each = 1,200 (432,000 human years at 360:1); ViP 4.24.33 gives 360,000 human years and 4.24.34 '1,200 divine years'. It begins when Kṛṣṇa departs (ViP 4.24.32; 5.38.8). Indian astronomy from Āryabhaṭa (499 CE: Kali 3600 in his 23rd year, AB 3.10) fixes its epoch at 3102 BCE, and the Aihole inscription of 634/635 CE counts 3,735 years since the Bhārata war.

sources.edition: GRETIL e-text, text of Kullūka (Shastri 1983) with Medhātithi variants
Critical edition, M. M. Pathak (Vadodara 1997–99); GRETIL e-text by P. Schreiner
sources.quote: trīṇi lakṣāṇi varṣāṇāṃ dvija mānuṣasaṃkhyayā / ṣaṣṭiṃ caiva sahasrāṇi bhaviṣyaty eṣa vai kaliḥ

note: The 3102 BCE epoch is an astronomical-traditional computation (Fleet 1911; Pingree 1981); it is not evidence for the date of any narrated event. The 360,000 of ViP 4.24.33 is recorded as the e-text reads. Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: End of Kali and advent of Kalki
description: Traditional chronology: at the junction closing the Kali age Kalki is born at Śambhala to Viṣṇuyaśas and restores the Kṛta age (BhP 1.3.25, 12.2.16–20; MatsP 47.247–251; AgP 16.7–10).

name: Āryabhaṭa's mahāyuga of equal quarters (alternative system)
description: Traditional chronology: in the Āryabhaṭīya a mahāyuga of 12,000 divine years (4,320,000 years) is divided into four equal yugapādas of 1,080,000 years, unlike the 4:3:2:1 Purāṇic proportions; a divine year is 360 solar years (AB 3.7–8).
note: An astronomical reworking of the traditional scheme. Traditional reckoning as stated in the cited texts; it is not a historical or scientific chronology and is not drawn on the same axis as scholarly dates.

name: Night of Brahmā (naimittika pralaya)
description: Traditional chronology: at the end of each day of Brahmā the three worlds are burned and flooded; Brahmā-Nārāyaṇa sleeps on the serpent for a night as long as the day (ViP 1.3.22–25; Manu 1.72–73; BhP 12.7.17).
